description: A tiny spark can kindle a great fire
summary: Flame Evidence Explorer is an AI-powered research assistant for NASA microgravity combustion studies. Users ask questions in English or Chinese. The system retrieves relevant NASA evidence, explains what the studies observed and under which conditions, and connects each claim to its cited evidence. In the FLEX case study, users can filter all 274 official test summaries, trace plotted values to their original CSV rows, and export a brief. For engineering education in Singapore, the explorer offers a bilingual classroom exercise: students can apply the same FLEX filters, compare interpretations, and check each claim against its source. The project makes AI explanations inspectable, giving learners and researchers a practical way to understand and compare combustion evidence.
details:
Flame Evidence Explorer is an AI-powered research assistant that turns NASA microgravity combustion literature into an interactive, source-linked investigation. Users can search BASS-II, Saffire IV/V, SAME-2, and FLEX in English or Chinese, compare their experimental conditions, and export evidence briefs.

The AI workflow starts by retrieving relevant curated NASA evidence for the user’s question. It then builds an explanation in the selected language, with evidence IDs attached to individual claims and study conditions stated alongside the results. The server validates each cited ID against the evidence supplied for that question. Readers can open those entries, inspect the source and measurement context, and export the explanation with its references. For example, the assistant can explain that the FLEX technical report covers the first 284 tests, while the interactive case uses 274 test summaries from the NASA PSI-69 experiment table. When the available evidence is insufficient, the interface identifies the gap and points users to literature search.

The FLEX case gives users a way to verify results directly. Select methanol, an initial gas mixture with O₂ and N₂ mole fractions of 0.21 and 0.79, and the Extinction outcome. This yields nine records. Eight list plottable visible-extinction diameters ranging from 0.81 to 2 mm. Each plotted value links to its original CSV row. The interface shows differences in ambient pressure and initial droplet diameter, and FLEX report Appendix A.1 explains when the authors used extrapolation. Users can download the filtered records and NASA’s original CSV.

A Singapore classroom use case connects the space research to local engineering education. Students can work through the FLEX example in English or Chinese, compare AI explanations, and check whether each cited source supports the observation. They can then identify the measurements they would need for a separate fire-safety study in an enclosed setting on Earth. This exercise turns source checking and experimental reasoning into practical skills.

The project uses HTML, CSS, JavaScript, and Python tooling. GitHub Pages hosts the explorer, and a Netlify function serves the AI explanation layer. The charts and filter summaries use the selected NASA records. Codex assisted code development, and OpenAI GPT assisted the initial abstract summaries and English demonstration script. Windows text-to-speech synthesized the narration.
